h1: Equal Highs and Lows: Reading Liquidity Pools
seoTitle: Equal Highs & Lows: Reading Liquidity Pools | LearnSMC
metaDescription: Learn how Equal Highs (EQH) and Equal Lows (EQL) form liquidity pools, why double tops fail, and how to define tick tolerance before chart replay.
quickAnswer: Equal Highs (EQH) and Equal Lows (EQL) are two or more swing highs or swing lows aligned within a predefined price tolerance, creating visible reference shelves where stop-losses and breakout orders frequently cluster.
takeaways: EQH and EQL rarely align to the exact tick—define an objective pip or tick tolerance and timeframe before marking pools in replay.
Traditional retail analysis treats EQH as double-top resistance, while SMC study treats the same level as a Buyside Liquidity (BSL) shelf.
Relative Equal Highs (slightly lower second high) and Relative Equal Lows (slightly higher second low) act like magnets because stops sit just beyond both extremes.
Sweeping EQH or EQL only triggers a reversal study when candle bodies reclaim back inside the range; sustained closes beyond the shelf indicate acceptance.

sections.title: 1. Double Top vs. Liquidity Pool: Why Equal Levels Fail So Often

blocks.text: When price stalls twice near the same ceiling, textbook retail patterns call it a double top and expect an immediate sell-off. Yet traders who short that second peak routinely place their stop-losses just a few ticks above the ceiling, while breakout traders place buy-stops at the very same height.

In Smart Money Concepts, that double top is labeled Equal Highs (EQH)—and its mirror-image double bottom is labeled Equal Lows (EQL). Instead of assuming the ceiling will hold forever, you treat the shelf as a high-visibility liquidity reference.

sections.title: 2. Exact vs. Relative EQH/EQL & Setting Predefined Tolerance

blocks.text: Waiting for two swings to match to the exact 0.0001 pip causes traders to miss most real-world pools. Defining a fixed tick or pip tolerance before replay prevents hindsight bias and keeps your chart labels consistent.

rows: Two or more highs/lows at virtually identical price
Clean visible shelf; attracts tight stop clustering
Second peak slightly lower (or second trough slightly higher)
Often swept together in a single expansion leg

sections.title: 4. How to Mark EQH and EQL Step by Step on a Blank Chart

items: Start on a higher timeframe (4H or 1H) so minor 1-minute noise does not distract you.
Locate two or more distinct swing highs or lows separated by a clear pullback.
Measure the vertical spread between peaks and confirm it sits inside your predefined tolerance.
Draw a horizontal ray to the right labeled EQH (BSL) or EQL (SSL) and wait for price to reach it.

sections.title: 7. EQH/EQL Pools vs. Single Swing Highs & Trendlines

blocks.text: A single swing high holds one group of stops, whereas Equal Highs stack multiple rounds of short stops and breakout orders along one horizontal line. Compared with diagonal trendlines, horizontal EQH/EQL shelves remain identical across zoom levels and chart scales.

sections.title: 8. When EQH/EQL Pools Form During the Trading Day

blocks.text: Equal Highs and Equal Lows appear most cleanly during Asian session consolidations, pre-market NY ranges (07:00–08:30 ET), and lunchtime pauses (12:00–13:30 ET) before volatility expands.

sections.title: 12. Frequently Asked Questions (Equal Highs & Equal Lows)

faqs.question: What are Equal Highs (EQH) and Equal Lows (EQL) in trading?
faqs.answer: Equal Highs (EQH) are two or more swing highs aligned at nearly the same price level, while Equal Lows (EQL) are two or more swing lows aligned at nearly the same level. Traders monitor them as visible liquidity references.

faqs.question: Do Equal Highs have to match to the exact tick?
faqs.answer: No. Real markets rarely align to the exact tick. Relative Equal Highs or Lows within a predefined tolerance (such as a few ticks on index futures or a few pips on FX) serve the same reference role.

faqs.question: Why do double tops and double bottoms often get swept?
faqs.answer: Because many traders place stop-losses just past the double top or bottom while breakout traders place stop entries at the same price, creating a concentrated cluster of buy-stops or sell-stops.

faqs.question: What confirms an EQH sweep versus a real breakout?
faqs.answer: A sweep pierces the EQH shelf and closes back inside the range (often followed by a lower-timeframe structure shift), whereas a real breakout closes and holds candle bodies above the shelf.
